details:
**The Birthday Party**
Pinter's first full-length play (1958) and the most common title clue for him. It is set in Meg and Petey Boles's seaside boarding house, where the boarder Stanley Webber, a former pianist, is terrorized by two mysterious visitors during a birthday party Meg throws for him.

**Goldberg and McCann**
The menacing pair (a Jewish man and an Irishman) who arrive at the boarding house in The Birthday Party. They interrogate Stanley with absurd questions such as "Why did you kill your wife?" and "Why did the chicken cross the road?", and at the end take a newly shaven Stanley, holding his broken glasses, away in a car to see "Monty."

**Blind man's buff and Lulu**
During the party game of blind man's buff in The Birthday Party, McCann breaks Stanley's glasses and Stanley gets his foot stuck in the toy drum Meg gave him. When the lights go out, Stanley tries to strangle Meg and then attacks Lulu, a young woman who earlier called him "a bit of a washout."

**"Don't let them tell you what to do!"**
Petey's line to Stanley as Goldberg and McCann lead him away at the end of The Birthday Party. The play ends with Petey not telling Meg that Stanley is gone, while she recalls being "the belle of the ball"; the play opens with Meg repeatedly asking Petey whether his cornflakes are "nice."

**The Dumb Waiter**
A one-act "comedy of menace" (1960) in which two hitmen wait in a basement room for orders. The title device, a food lift, keeps sending down orders for elaborate dishes such as "Macaroni Pastitsio" and "Ormitha Macarounada," which the men cannot fill, and they reply through a speaking tube.

**Ben and Gus and "light the kettle"**
The two hitmen of The Dumb Waiter. They argue over whether one says "light the kettle" or "put on the kettle," Ben reads newspaper stories aloud (including an old man run over by a lorry), and Gus fusses over the toilet that won't flush. At the end, Ben is told through the speaking tube to kill the next man to enter, and that man is Gus.

**Comedy of menace**
The label critics applied to Pinter's early plays, borrowed by the critic Irving Wardle from the subtitle of David Campton's play The Lunatic View. The term describes plays in which everyday, often comic dialogue hides an unexplained threat.

**Betrayal**
Pinter's 1978 play about the affair between Emma and Jerry, the best friend of Emma's husband Robert. Its nine scenes mostly run in reverse chronological order, starting after the affair has ended; one scene recalls Robert's trip to Torcello near Venice, where he read Yeats alone, and Robert also declines to play squash with Jerry.

**The Caretaker**
Pinter's 1960 play in which Aston takes the homeless Davies (who goes by the alias Bernard Jenkins) into his junk-filled room. Davies keeps putting off a trip to Sidcup to retrieve his identity papers, Aston gives a monologue about the electroshock treatment he got in a mental hospital, and his brother Mick smashes a Buddha statue near the end.

**The Homecoming**
A 1965 play in which Teddy, a philosophy professor living in America, brings his wife Ruth to meet his family in North London. Ruth ends up staying behind with Teddy's father Max and his brothers, apparently to work as a prostitute, while Teddy returns to America alone, and Teddy's uncle Sam collapses on the floor.

**Memory plays (Old Times, No Man's Land, A Kind of Alaska)**
Pinter's later plays focused on memory. In Old Times, Anna visits Deeley and his wife Kate, who says "I remember you dead"; in No Man's Land, the drunken writer Hirst brings Spooner home from a pub; in A Kind of Alaska, Deborah wakes from a 29-year sleeping-sickness coma (some questions say 30) and is cared for by Hornby.

**A Slight Ache**
A play first written for radio (1959) in which Edward and his wife Flora become obsessed with a silent, possibly deaf, matchseller standing outside their gate. At the end Flora hands Edward's tray of matches to him and takes the matchseller in, replacing her husband.

**Pinter pauses**
The famous silences and "pauses" written into Pinter's stage directions. They leave much unsaid in his characters' speech and are a defining feature of his style, seen in characters such as Aston in The Caretaker.

**Political plays (One for the Road, Ashes to Ashes)**
Later plays about torture and state violence. In One for the Road, the interrogator Nicolas taunts his prisoners, including the boy Nicky; Ashes to Ashes is a dialogue between Rebecca and Devlin haunted by memories of atrocities.

**David Baron and the Nobel Prize**
Pinter acted under the stage name David Baron early in his career. He won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Literature.
